chunks: As for what was narrated by ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥasan, from ʿAlī ibn Asbāṭ, from his paternal uncle Yaʿqūb al-Aḥmar, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

If menstruation comes upon a woman in the month of Ramadan before zawāl, then she has latitude to eat and drink. But if it comes upon her after the sun’s decline, then she should perform ghusl and count the fast of that day, so long as she has not eaten or drunk.

So this report is an error from the narrator, because if seeing blood is what breaks the fast, then it is not permissible for her to count the fast of that day. Rather, it is only recommended for her to refrain for the rest of the day as a matter of discipline if she sees blood after zawāl. And that which indicates this is what...

key_terms.بِصَوْمِ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمِ: as the fast of that day being counted
key_terms.تَأْدِيبًا: as a disciplinary or educative restraint
key_terms.شَهْرِ رَمَضَانَ: the month of Ramadan in the context of obligatory fasting

ai.seo_question: If a woman begins menstruation during a fast in Ramadan, does that day still count as a valid fast?
ai.summary: This passage discusses the ruling of a woman who begins menstruation during a day of Ramadan and then critiques a transmitted report attributed to the narrator. It states that menstruation invalidates the fast upon the appearance of blood, and that if this occurs after zawāl, she should only refrain from eating for the rest of the day as a recommended act of discipline, not count it as a valid fast.
